# Removing Tailgate Struts Without C-Clips: A Practical Guide

When working on a 2006 Honda Odyssey, specifically Japanese imports circulating in markets like New Zealand, you often encounter tailgate struts that deviate from standard assembly norms. The conventional method involves locating the internal C-clip within the strut housing, loosening it with a pick tool, and snapping the piston out. However, on many units of this vintage, the factory omitted this retaining clip entirely. This design choice simplifies manufacturing but complicates disassembly for owners attempting repairs or upgrades. Without that mechanical latch, you cannot simply pop the strut out; instead, you must manage the hydraulic resistance and structural integrity of the gas spring to extract it safely.

The core challenge lies in the physics of a sealed gas strut. These components function as one-way valves: they allow air into the cylinder when compressed but seal tightly when extended. In the absence of a C-clip, the piston is held in place by friction and internal pressure. If you attempt to pull directly on the rod end without addressing these forces, you risk bending the piston rod or shearing the mounting bolts that secure the strut to the tailgate hinges.

To remove the strut effectively, you need to release the hydraulic pressure holding the piston in its extended position. The most reliable approach involves installing a temporary bypass valve or utilizing a specific tool designed to vent the nitrogen charge. Many mechanics use a "strut venting tool" that screws into the base of the strut near the mount point. Once attached, you carefully bleed off the internal gas until the rod can be pushed back slightly or pulled free with manageable force.

If specialized venting tools are unavailable, an alternative involves drilling a small hole through the rubber boot at the base of the strut, though this is less ideal as it compromises the seal permanently. A safer bet without compromising the new part later is to use a long needle valve or a makeshift setup involving a bicycle pump and a check valve temporarily rigged to vent pressure slowly. The goal is to reduce internal pressure just enough so that the mechanical friction becomes the only resistance, allowing you to unthread the mounting nuts or bolts.

Once the pressure is bled, you must support the tailgate weight carefully. Remove the lower retaining bolt or nut first, as this often releases the final lock holding the piston in place. Be prepared for the rod to retract abruptly once the hydraulic hold is gone. It is advisable to have an assistant hold the tailgate or use a prop bar to prevent the door from slamming shut unexpectedly while you manipulate the strut internals.

When installing the replacement strut, ensure you reverse the process carefully. If your new struts also lack C-clips, you will simply thread the piston into the housing until it seats firmly against the internal shoulder. However, if you are mixing old and new parts, or if the new unit requires a clip, verify compatibility with the specific 2006 Odyssey Japanese import chassis before final assembly.

There is also a consideration regarding the rubber seals inside the strut. If the original struts were removed without bleeding pressure properly, the internal O-rings may have been damaged by the sudden release of nitrogen or physical impact. Inspect these seals upon opening the housing; if they show signs of deformation, replacing the entire strut assembly rather than just rebuilding it is often the more cost-effective long-term decision.

For those managing inventory or looking for a streamlined solution in New Zealand automotive circles, checking local suppliers who specialize in Japanese import parts can yield struts pre-configured with easier removal mechanisms. While modifying an existing unit takes time and specific tools, sourcing a compatible replacement that matches your original specification ensures you maintain the factory's intended balance without needing to fabricate custom venting solutions every time a service is required.
